questions.title: How exactly does the '1.58' bit count arise from ternary {-1, 0, 1} weights?
questions.question_body: The abstract states that BitNet b1.58 has ternary weights taking values of {-1, 0, 1}, yet calls it a '1.58-bit' model. Intuitively, I know that representing three distinct states requires $	ext{log}_2(3)$ bits per weight, which is approximately 1.5849... However, the paper mentions adding a '0' to the original 1-bit BitNet. Does this mean the original BitNet was strictly binary {-1, 1}? If so, why does introducing the zero state increase the theoretical information density to ~1.58 bits rather than just keeping it at a lower effective bit rate due to sparsity? I want to confirm if this terminology refers purely to the entropy of the distribution or if there's a specific encoding scheme implied.

questions.title: Clarification on activation scaling ranges: [-Qb, Qb] vs [0, Qb]
questions.question_body: In the section describing Quantization Functions, the authors mention that unlike previous implementations (like standard BitNet), they scale activations to $[-Q_b, Q_b]$ instead of $[0, Q_b]$ to avoid zero-point quantization. My confusion lies in how this affects the subsequent ReLU-like operations within SwiGLU or other non-linearities. If activations are centered around zero without shifting them to positive integers first, doesn't this change how the 'integer-only' matrix multiplication interacts with the gating mechanisms? Specifically, how does an integer-based GEMM handle inputs that include negative values when passed into a SwiGLU layer designed for standard floating point logic?

questions.title: Is the 'new scaling law' empirical or derived from first principles?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that BitNet b1.58 defines a 'new scaling law' where efficiency gains (latency/memory/energy) grow disproportionately compared to FP16 models as size increases (e.g., 70B is much more efficient relative to its FP counterpart than smaller models). Is this observed behavior simply a consequence of fixed overheads becoming negligible as model size grows (standard asymptotic analysis), or does the removal of multiplications fundamentally alter the exponent in Chinchilla-style scaling laws? I am trying to determine if this implies we need fewer total training tokens for large-scale BitNets compared to LLaMA-sized counterparts to reach similar perplexity.

questions.title: What is the mechanism behind 'feature filtering' provided by zeros?
questions.question_body: The authors state that including 0 in the weights provides explicit support for 'feature filtering,' which improves performance over strict binary (-1/+1) models. Conceptually, I understand that setting a weight to zero effectively turns off a connection (similar to dropout or sparse attention). However, in dense matrix multiplication where every neuron connects to every other neuron via these ternary weights, how does this differ from simply having very small weights in FP models? Why is an exact zero in an integer domain considered qualitatively different for feature selection compared to near-zero floating point numbers?
